{{Short description|Theorem bounding the growth rate of analytic functions}}
{{about|Nachbin's theorem on complex analysis|Nachbin's theorem on approximation theory|Stone–Weierstrass theorem#Nachbin's theorem}}

In [[mathematics]], in the area of [[complex analysis]], '''Nachbin's theorem''' (named after [[Leopoldo Nachbin]]) is a result used to establish bounds on the growth rates for [[analytic function|analytic functions]]. In particular, Nachbin's theorem may be used to give the domain of convergence of the '''generalized Borel transform''', also called '''Nachbin summation'''. 

This article provides a brief review of growth rates, including the idea of a '''function of exponential type'''. Classification of growth rates based on type help provide a finer tool than [[big O notation|big O]] or [[Landau notation]], since a number of theorems about the analytic structure of the bounded function and its [[integral transform]]s can be stated. 

==Exponential type==
{{Main|Exponential type}}
A function <math>f(z)</math> defined on the [[complex plane]] is said to be of exponential type if there exist constants <math>M</math> and <math>\alpha</math> such that

:<math>|f(re^{i\theta})|\le Me^{\alpha r}</math>

in the limit of <math>r\to\infty</math>. Here, the [[complex variable]] <math>z</math> was written as <math>z=re^{i\theta}</math> to emphasize that the limit must hold in all directions <math>\theta</math>.  Letting <math>\alpha</math> stand for the [[infimum]] of all such <math>\alpha</math>, one then says that the function <math>f</math> is of ''exponential type <math>\alpha</math>''.

For example, let <math>f(z)=\sin(\pi z)</math>. Then one says that <math>\sin(\pi z)</math> is of exponential type <math>\pi</math>, since <math>\pi</math> is the smallest number that bounds the growth of <math>\sin(\pi z)</math> along the imaginary axis. So, for this example, [[Carlson's theorem]] cannot apply, as it requires functions of exponential type less than <math>\pi</math>.

==&Psi; type==
Additional function types may be defined for other bounding functions besides the exponential function. In general, a function <math>\Psi(t)</math> is a '''comparison function''' if it has a series

:<math>\Psi(t)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \Psi_n t^n</math>

with <math>\Psi_n>0</math> for all <math>n</math>, and

:<math>\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\Psi_{n+1}}{\Psi_n} = 0.</math>

Comparison functions are necessarily [[entire function|entire]], which follows from the [[ratio test]]. If <math>\Psi(t)</math> is such a comparison function, one then says that <math>f</math> is of <math>\Psi</math>-type if there exist constants <math>M</math> and <math>\tau</math> such that

:<math>\left|f\left(re^{i\theta}\right)\right| \le M\Psi(\tau r)</math>

as <math>r\to \infty</math>. If <math>\tau</math> is the infimum of all such <math>\tau</math> one says that <math>f</math> is of <math>\Psi</math>-type <math>\tau</math>.

Nachbin's theorem states that a function <math>f(z)</math> with the series

:<math>f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n z^n</math>

is of <math>\Psi</math>-type <math>\tau</math> if and only if

:<math>\limsup_{n\to\infty} \left| \frac{f_n}{\Psi_n} \right|^{1/n} = \tau.</math>
This is naturally connected to the [[root test]] and can be considered a relative of the [[Cauchy–Hadamard theorem]].

==Generalized Borel transform==
Nachbin's theorem has immediate applications in [[Cauchy's integral formula|Cauchy theorem]]-like situations, and for [[integral transforms]].  For example, the '''generalized Borel transform''' is given by

:<math>F(w)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{f_n}{\Psi_n w^{n+1}}.</math>

If <math>f</math> is of <math>\Psi</math>-type <math>\tau</math>, then the exterior of the domain of convergence of <math>F(w)</math>, and all of its singular points, are contained within the disk

:<math>|w| \le \tau.</math>

Furthermore, one has

:<math>f(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_\gamma \Psi (zw) F(w)\, dw</math>

where the [[contour of integration]] γ encircles the disk <math>|w| \le \tau</math>.  This generalizes the usual '''Borel transform''' for functions of exponential type, where <math>\Psi(t)=e^t</math>.  The integral form for the generalized Borel transform follows as well. Let <math>\alpha(t)</math> be a function whose first derivative is bounded on the interval <math>[0,\infty)</math> and that satisfies the defining equation

:<math>\frac{1}{\Psi_n} = \int_0^\infty t^n\, d\alpha(t)</math>

where <math>d\alpha(t)=\alpha^{\prime}(t)\,dt</math>. Then the integral form of the generalized Borel transform is

:<math>F(w)=\frac{1}{w} \int_0^\infty f \left(\frac{t}{w}\right) \, d\alpha(t).</math>

The ordinary Borel transform is regained by setting <math>\alpha(t)=-e^{-t}</math>. Note that the integral form of the Borel transform is the [[Laplace transform]].

==Nachbin summation==
Nachbin summation can be used to sum divergent series that [[Borel summation]] does not, for instance to [[Asymptotic solution|asymptotically solve]] integral equations of the form:

:<math> g(s)=s\int_0^\infty K(st) f(t)\,dt </math>

where <math display="inline"> g(s)= \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n s^{-n} </math>, <math>f(t)</math> may or may not be of exponential type, and the kernel <math>K(u)</math> has a [[Mellin transform]]. The solution can be obtained using Nachbin summation as <math> f(x)= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{a_n}{M(n+1)}x^n </math> with the <math> a_n </math> from <math> g(s) </math> and with <math>M(n)</math> the Mellin transform of <math>K(u)</math>. An example of this is the Gram series  <math> \pi (x) \approx 1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\log^{n}(x)}{n\cdot n!\zeta (n+1)}.</math>

In some cases as an extra condition we require <math> \int_0^\infty K(t)t^{n}\,dt </math> to be finite and nonzero for <math>n=0,1,2,3,....</math>

==Fréchet space==
Collections of functions of exponential type <math>\tau</math> can form a [[complete space|complete]] [[uniform space]], namely a [[Fréchet space]], by the [[topological space|topology]] induced by the countable family of [[norm (mathematics)|norm]]s

:<math> \|f\|_{n} = \sup_{z \in \mathbb{C}} \exp \left[-\left(\tau + \frac{1}{n}\right)|z|\right]|f(z)|.</math>
